title: why the hard moment weighs more
subtitle: how the mind keeps score of what went badly

steps.prompt: what small change in grammar can give a bit of distance?
steps.answer: using a name, or "you", instead of "i". it's the distance a friend has.

steps.text: picture a day with nine good moments and one awkward one.
which one is most likely to replay tonight?

options.label: the awkward one
options.reply: most people say that one. it's very common.

options.label: a couple of the good ones
honestly, all of it
options.reply: fair. some days are like that.

steps.text: a large review found that in many areas of life, bad events tend to leave a stronger mark than good ones of the same size. researchers call it the negativity bias.
it likely helped once. noticing trouble fast kept people safe. it's the mind doing a job.
the catch is that good moments can go uncounted, unless we help count them.

steps.prompt: which of these usually go uncounted? pick any:
steps.reply: those count. they're real, and they happened.

steps.text: the mind holds on to hard moments more than good ones. noticing the good moments helps them count too.
steps.evidence: strong for the bias itself (a large review); counting good moments is our suggestion, not tested here

steps.text: tonight, name one thing that went okay today. just one, said plainly.

grounding.idea: bad events tend to outweigh good ones of similar size across many areas of life
